top_level_objectives: Use Lewis structures to count electron domains around a central atom.
Relate electron-pair repulsion to the five fundamental electron-domain geometries.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry when lone pairs are present.
Predict common molecular shapes and approximate bond-angle trends using VSEPR theory.
Compare VSEPR predictions with representative real molecules such as H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, and XeF4.

scenes.scene_name: From Lewis Structure to Electron Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce how a Lewis structure is translated into a count of bonding regions and lone pairs around a central atom.
key_visuals: A 2D Lewis structure beside a central atom surrounded by highlighted electron domains
Bonding pairs and lone pairs shown as separate colored regions
A simple domain counter updating as examples are inspected
student_actions: Identify the central atom in a displayed molecule
Count bonding domains and lone-pair domains from the Lewis structure
State the total number of electron domains before predicting shape

scenes.brief_purpose: Build the core VSEPR idea that electron pairs arrange themselves to minimize repulsion in three dimensions.
key_visuals: Movable electron domains around a central atom that push apart as they are added
A transition from crowded arrangements to stable low-repulsion arrangements
Angle labels appearing as domains settle into place
student_actions: Drag electron domains around the central atom
Release them to watch the arrangement relax into a minimum-repulsion geometry
Describe how increasing the number of domains changes the spatial arrangement

scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the ideal geometries for two through six electron domains as the foundation for later shape predictions.
key_visuals: Side-by-side 3D models of linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral arrangements
Ideal bond angles labeled on each model
student_actions: Match a given number of electron domains to its ideal electron-domain geometry
Rotate each 3D arrangement to inspect its symmetry
Compare ideal bond angles across the five base geometries

scenes.scene_name: How Lone Pairs Change Molecular Shape
scenes.brief_purpose: Show how removing terminal atoms from the visual while keeping lone pairs leads from electron-domain geometry to molecular geometry.
key_visuals: An electron-domain geometry overlaid with visible lone pairs and bonded atoms
Progressive examples transforming tetrahedral to trigonal pyramidal and bent, trigonal bipyramidal to seesaw and T-shaped, and octahedral to square pyramidal and square planar
A panel contrasting electron-domain geometry with molecular geometry names
student_actions: Hide lone pairs from the outer-shape view while keeping them in the repulsion model
Name the resulting molecular geometry for each example
Explain why electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry can differ

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate that lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and compress bond angles from ideal values.
key_visuals: A comparison of methane and water with angle measurements highlighted
Lone-pair clouds shown larger than bonding regions around the central atom
Animated compression of bond angles as lone pairs are introduced
student_actions: Compare the tetrahedral angle in methane to the smaller H-O-H angle in water
Predict whether adding lone pairs will increase or decrease bond angles
Relate observed angle changes to stronger lone-pair repulsions

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate the full prediction workflow by applying VSEPR to representative molecules from the course.
key_visuals: Interactive models of H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, and XeF4
A stepwise checklist: Lewis structure, domain count, electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, bond-angle estimate
A comparison view pairing predicted shapes with observed molecular structures
student_actions: Work through the VSEPR steps for each displayed molecule
Assign both electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry
Check predictions against the molecule models and summarize recurring patterns
